body.hook: Playing the right notes is only the start. To play a piece truly well, you need to know where it comes from: who wrote it, when, why, and what style it calls for. That knowledge shapes every choice you make.

study.title: Know Your Piece
study.question: How does research shape performance?
study.passage:
Research guide (written for this lesson):
Style periods (approximate): Baroque (about 1600–1750): steady tempos, terraced dynamics (sudden loud/soft), ornaments. Classical (about 1750–1820): balance, clear phrases, elegance. Romantic (about 1820–1900): expressive, rubato, big dynamic range. 20th century and beyond: varied styles, changing meters, new sounds.
Band history examples: Gustav Holst's First Suite in E♭ for Military Band (composed 1909) helped establish serious original music for concert band; Percy Grainger's Lincolnshire Posy (1937) is based on English folk songs.
Research questions for your solo or ensemble piece: Who is the composer and when did they live? What era or style is the piece? Why was it written (event, folk song, commission)? What does the title mean? What do tempo and expression markings tell you?
Sources: the score's notes, publisher's website, library database, reliable encyclopedias.
Programme note (100–150 words): composer, background, what to listen for. No copied text; cite sources.
discussion: What surprised you about your piece's history?
How does the era affect how you should play it?
What will you tell the audience to listen for?
study.product: Write a 100–150 word programme note for your piece with sources, and explain two performance choices your research suggests.

body.objective: Students will be able to make interpretive choices.
successCriteria: I can make interpretive choices about tempo, dynamics, phrasing and tone
I can justify choices using the score and research
I can mark and perform my interpretation consistently
body.hook: Give five great musicians the same piece and you'll hear five different performances. Each makes choices about tempo, dynamics, phrasing and tone. Interpretation is where you add your own voice.

vocabulary.definition: Expressive stretching and pushing of tempo.
Feeling and meaning shown through musical choices.
How phrases are shaped and connected.
The quality of sound, such as bright or dark.
A pencil note in the music showing a performance choice.

study.title: Making It Yours
study.question: How do I make and justify interpretive choices?
study.passage:
Interpretation workshop (written for this lesson):
1. What the composer wrote: list tempo, dynamics, articulations and expression words (e.g. dolce = sweetly; espressivo = expressively; maestoso = majestic). These are the frame.
2. What's open to you: exact tempo within a range; size of dynamic changes; where phrases peak; tone colour; small rubato at phrase ends (if suited to the style); length of fermatas and breaths.
3. Listen to two recordings of a piece (or two classmates); list three differences.
4. Make choices for your piece: write at least five interpretive markings in pencil (e.g. "peak here," "warmer tone," "slight rit.").
5. Justify each: "I chose a slight ritardando in bar 16 because it ends the A section and the style is Romantic."
6. Consistency: play it twice; are your choices the same both times? Performers practise interpretation just like notes.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
discussion: What differences did you hear between two performances?
Which of your choices is most personal?
How did research support your choices?
Were your choices consistent across two run-throughs?
study.product: Mark at least five interpretive choices in your piece, justify each in writing, and perform it consistently.

successCriteria: I can perform a prepared piece with expression and stage presence

body.hook: The final performance brings everything together: technique, reading, ensemble skills and interpretation. Afterwards, honest self-assessment is what turns one performance into the next level.

study.title: Final Performance
study.question: How do I perform at my best and learn from it?
study.passage:
Performance guide (written for this lesson):
Nerves are normal: a racing heart is your body preparing. Strategies: slow breathing (in 4, hold 4, out 6); a pre-performance routine (warm up, tune, check music, three slow breaths); positive self-talk ("I've prepared this"); focus on the music's message, not on mistakes.
Performance (solo or ensemble): walk on with confidence; introduce the piece with your programme note highlight; perform your interpretation; acknowledge applause with a bow.
Recording review: listen back with the music and rate 1–4: tone, technique, rhythm, intonation, expression and interpretation, stage presence. For each rating, write evidence with a bar number.
SMART goal: e.g. "Within four weeks, play the chromatic scale over two octaves at 100 BPM in sixteenths with even tone."
Reflection: what you're proudest of across the year, and your plan for continuing music.
